prize_parts.citation: for the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis using reversible-terminator chemistry on clonal surface arrays

statement.case_for: Massively parallel sequencing is a chemistry invention in its core: reversible 3'-blocked fluorescent terminators, surface-bound clonal cluster amplification and single-molecule-level optical readout. It has changed the scale at which biology and medicine can be done, from genomics and cancer diagnostics to ancient DNA and infectious disease surveillance, and has been confirmed independently on every platform for roughly two decades. There is no question of maturity. After careful reading of colleagues' attribution arguments I narrow my opening three names to the Solexa pair, Balasubramanian and Klenerman, who conceived and built the chemistry and the single-molecule/cluster readout that became the dominant technology. This gives a clean, defensible two-person prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the field's credit is split across at least three lineages (Solexa, 454/pyrosequencing, Lynx/Mayer clonal arrays, plus Ju's terminator chemistry), and leaving out Rothberg and Mayer will be contested. A second concern is categorical: some members may see this as genomics tooling or technology rather than chemistry, and the 1980 prize for Sanger and Gilbert sequencing makes a repeat of the theme harder to argue. I also hold my attribution partly from memory of the history, so I would want the committee's documentary evidence on priority before this is final.

responses.point: Johan ranks Pd-catalyzed C-N cross-coupling first as a mature, clearly original, widely used reaction with Buchwald and Hartwig as the natural two laureates, and notes it sits next to the 2010 prize without being redundant.
responses.response: I agree this is the cleanest attribution on the list and the broadest industrial footprint, and it is a serious rival to my own choice; that three colleagues put it first deserves weight. My reservation is distinctive-ness: for a non-synthetic chemist the step from the 2010 cross-coupling prize is smaller than the step from classical sequencing to massively parallel sequencing, and the Kosugi precedence question has not gone away. I do not think the support for B065 shows it is more important than B037, but I would not resist it if the committee converges there, which is why I list it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Andrei ranks sequencing second and argues the Solexa pair (Balasubramanian and Klenerman) is the most defensible allocation, with reversible terminators and cluster readout as the decisive invention, while noting the risk that the committee sees it as biology rather than chemistry.
responses.response: I accept his narrower allocation and have moved to it from my opening trio; dropping Mayer makes the citation more precise and avoids a diffuse priority fight. I disagree only mildly on the chemistry-versus-biology risk: the novelty here is the terminator and surface chemistry and the single-molecule detection, not the biology it later enabled, so I think the chemistry classification is secure. His support is useful because he works directly with these data and judges the impact first-hand.

responses.point: Peter places C-N coupling first and argues that recognition is overdue after three decades of use, while he ranks targeted protein degradation third, saying the glue and PROTAC strands have distinct credit.
responses.response: I agree with him that maturity is a point in favour of coupling chemistry, but sequencing has the same maturity and a far larger effect outside chemistry. On degraders, I share his concern that with up to eight credited names a three-person prize forces arbitrary cuts, and I take this as a real reason to prefer B037, where a two-person core is easier to justify.

responses.point: Daniel puts protein degradation first because heterobifunctional degraders and glues are a new drug modality that rewrote the explanation of thalidomide, and he accepts that the lack of an approved PROTAC means timing is early.
responses.response: The conceptual argument is strong and I rated it third myself. But I weigh the missing approved PROTAC more heavily than he does, and the PROTAC/cereblon-glue split means a single prize either bundles two strands or leaves out Handa or Ciulli. Sequencing has finished proving itself, which for a prize that rewards lasting benefit counts for more than promise.

uncertainties: Whether Rothberg (454) and Mayer deserve inclusion, which would turn a two-person Solexa prize into a contested three-person one.
Whether a majority will regard massively parallel sequencing as chemistry rather than genomics technology after the 1980 sequencing prize.
Whether the committee prefers the broader mature organic-synthesis candidate B065, which has more opening first-place votes than any other ballot.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I am an experimental nanophysicist at Lund with no documented working relationship with Balasubramanian, Klenerman or the other candidates; as chair I take care not to let my own opening first-place ranking steer the discussion.
